Manufacturers: same (applicant and manufacturer — KERN & SOHN GmbH)

Certified type:
- Category: "Non-automatic weighing instrument" — the schema example categories are like "Load cell", "Indicator", ... For NAWE I'd use "Non-automatic weighing instrument".
- type_designations: ["TPCJ-A"]
- module_designation: not applicable — omit or "Not applicable"? The schema says module_designation: "Analog load cell" | "Not applicable" | null. Not mentioned, so omit (don't fabricate). Actually maybe null. I'll omit.
- description: null / omit

Model family: only one model TPCJ-A; the max capacity is a range 0 ≤ Max ≤ 600 g, single interval. Not a family — omit model_family.

Characteristics (type_level):
- accuracy_class: "(II)" — value "II" perhaps. Value could be string "(II)" or "II". I'll use value "II". Hmm, the cert says accuracy class ⦿(II). Canonical label: accuracy_class, value: "II". Unit null.
- maximum_capacity: 0 ≤ Max ≤ 600 g → value {min: 0, max: 600}, unit "g". Hmm, Max is the maximum capacity; "0 ≤ Max ≤ 600 g" means the maximum capacity can range from 0 to 600 g — this covers a family of capacities up to 600 g? Actually for this type, Max ranges up to 600 g. Could be interpreted as the type covers instruments with Max from 0 to 600 g. I'll encode value {min: 0, max: 600}, unit_symbol "g". Alternatively max_capacity: {min: null, max: 600}. The text literally "0 ≤ Max ≤ 600 g". I'll keep {min: 0, max: 600}.
- verification_scale_interval: e ≥ 0.1 g → value {min: 0.1, max: null}, unit "g".
- actual_scale_interval: e = 10 d → value "10 d"? Hmm. Actual scale interval e = 10 d, meaning e equals 10 times d. This is a relation. Could encode as value 10, unit "d" with reference? I'd do attribute actual_scale_interval, value "10 d" string, or value 10 unit "d". The rule says formulas/symbols kept as strings. "10 d" — d is the display division. I'll do {"value": 10, "unit_symbol": "d"}? Hmm, d is not really a unit but scale interval unit. Safer: value "10 d" string? I think {"value": 10, "unit_symbol": "d"} is acceptable — d is the verification... Actually d is the actual scale interval unit (displayed division). I'll use value 10, unit "d". Hmm, but could be noisy. Let me use "value": "10 d", unit null? The strict rule: separate numeric from unit. 10 is numeric, d is the unit-ish. I'll go value: 10, unit_symbol: "d", unit_id: null.

Actually wait — "Actual scale interval e = 10 d" — hmm, that means e (verification interval) equals 10 × d (actual). Hmm, typically e ≥ d; here e = 10d. So value 10 relative to d. I'll encode as attribute actual_scale_interval_ratio? Keep label canonical: actual_scale_interval. Value: "10 d"? Let me just do {"value": 10, "unit_symbol": "d"}.

- weighing_range: "Single interval" → value "Single interval", string. Canonical label: weighing_range. value: "single interval" — keep as "Single interval".
- maximum_number_of_scale_intervals: n ≤ 6000 (one weighing range) → label max_scale_intervals? Canonical from rule 1 example: `Max. number of load cell intervals n<sub>LC</sub>` → `max_load_cell_intervals_nlc`. Here "Maximum number of scale intervals (one weighing range)" → `maximum_number_of_scale_intervals`. Value {min: null, max: 6000}, unit null.
- temperature_range: 15 °C / 30 °C → value {min: 15, max: 30}, unit "°C". Label temperature_range.
- Power supply: "100 – 240 V AC 50/60 Hz" plus "4x 1,5 V AA battery" plus "Rechargeable 3,7 V, 3700mAh Li-battery".
  - power_supply_voltage: {min: 100, max: 240}, unit "V"
  - power_supply_frequency: {min: 50, max: 60}, unit "Hz"
  - power_supply_type: "AC"
  - battery: 4x 1.5 V AA battery → power_supply_battery_voltage: value 1.5, unit "V"; battery_count: 4; battery_type: "AA". Also rechargeable 3.7 V, 3700 mAh Li-battery → battery_voltage 3.7 V, capacity 3700 mAh, type "Li".
  
  This is getting multi-valued. Maybe create components for power supply options? Simpler: type_level entries:
  - power_supply_voltage: {min 100, max 240} V
  - power_supply_frequency: {min 50, max 60} Hz
  - power_supply_type: "AC"
  - battery_voltage: 1.5 V, footnote none; battery_type "AA"; battery_quantity 4
  - rechargeable_battery_voltage: 3.7 V; rechargeable_battery_capacity: 3700 mAh; rechargeable_battery_type: "Li"
  
  Maybe combine into one attribute "power_supply" with string value? The rules prefer structured. I'll include the AC mains and battery entries as separate characteristics. Since there are two battery options, I could do config_level with axis "power_supply_source": values: mains / AA battery / rechargeable Li battery. That seems elegant:

  config_level: [
    {
      attribute: "power_supply_voltage",
      axis: "power_source",
      values: [
        {condition: "AC mains", value: {min:100,max:240}, unit_symbol: "V"},
        {condition: "AA battery (4x)", value: 1.5, unit_symbol: "V"},  // hmm 4x1.5 = 6V total? "4x 1,5 V AA battery" — 4 batteries of 1.5V each.
        {condition: "Rechargeable Li battery", value: 3.7, unit_symbol: "V"}
      ]
    }
  ]

  That may be over-engineering. But it captures the variation. Alternatively keep simple type_level entries. I think I'll do:

  type_level:
  - power_supply_voltage: {min:100, max:240} V
  - power_supply_frequency: {min:50, max:60} Hz
  - power_supply_type: "AC"
  - battery: maybe "4x 1,5 V AA battery" string and "Rechargeable 3,7 V, 3700mAh Li-battery" string.

  Hmm. Rules say lists of values are model matrix... These are alternative power sources. I'll use config_level with axis "power_source" for voltage, and add capacity where relevant. Let me do:

  config_level: [
    {
      "attribute": "power_supply",
      "axis": "power_source",
      "values": [
        {"condition": "AC mains", "value": {min:100, max:240}, "unit_symbol": "V"},
        ...
      ]
    }
  ]

  That mixes frequency. Maybe cleaner:

  config_level entries:
  1. attribute "power_supply_voltage", axis "power_source": AC mains 100–240 V; AA battery 1.5 V (4 cells); rechargeable Li battery 3.7 V.
  2. attribute "power_supply_frequency", axis "power_source": AC mains 50–60 Hz; others null? Skip nulls — only include condition where applicable.
  3. attribute "battery_capacity", axis "power_source": rechargeable Li 3700 mAh.

  Alternatively simpler: type_level with battery entries. I think I'll do both AC mains in type_level (primary) and battery alternatives in config_level. Hmm.

  Actually simplest defensible: type_level for mains (voltage, frequency, type), and two battery characteristics:
  - battery_type: "AA"
  - battery_cell_count: 4
  - battery_voltage: 1.5 V
  - rechargeable_battery_type: "Li"
  - rechargeable_battery_voltage: 3.7 V
  - rechargeable_battery_capacity: 3700 mAh

  That's many entries but precise. But battery_voltage vs rechargeable_battery_voltage ambiguous. Use labels: "battery_aa_voltage"? Eh. I'll use:
  - primary_battery_type: "AA"
  - primary_battery_count: 4
  - primary_battery_cell_voltage: 1.5 V
  - rechargeable_battery_type: "Li"
  - rechargeable_battery_voltage: 3.7 V
  - rechargeable_battery_capacity: 3700 "mAh"

  Hmm "unit_id" fields. Fine.

  Alternatively config_level. Let me weigh: the schema supports config_level for exactly this (attributes varying by configuration — alternative power sources). I'll use config_level:

  "config_level": [
    {
      "attribute": "power_supply_voltage",
      "axis": "power_source",
      "values": [
        {"condition": "AC mains", "value": {"min": 100, "max": 240}, "unit_symbol": "V"},
        {"condition": "4x AA battery", "value": 1.5, "unit_symbol": "V"},
        {"condition": "Rechargeable Li battery", "value": 3.7, "unit_symbol": "V"}
      ]
    },
    {
      "attribute": "power_supply_frequency",
      "axis": "power_source",
      "values": [
        {"condition": "AC mains", "value": {"min": 50, "max": 60}, "unit_symbol": "Hz"}
      ]
    },
    {
      "attribute": "rechargeable_battery_capacity",
      "axis": "power_source",
      "values": [
        {"condition": "Rechargeable Li battery", "value": 3700, "unit_symbol": "mAh"}
      ]
    }
  ]

  And type_level "power_supply_type": "AC". Hmm but AC only applies to mains. Fine — condition is "AC mains" for voltage/frequency, so power_supply_type maybe redundant. I could include type in condition string: "AC mains". Good.

  Also "4x 1,5 V AA battery" — note decimal comma: 1,5 → 1.5; 3,7 → 3.7.

- software_identification: "A1.0.02" → attribute software_identification, value "A1.0.02".

Recommendation:
- id: "R76" (canonical), edition: 2006? The schema: id (e.g. "R60"), edition (int). "OIML R 76-1:2006" — edition 2006, and part 1. Maybe id "R76-1"? Canonical "R76" with edition 2006; part info could be in id "R76-1". Hmm. The recommendation is R 76-1:2006. I'll set id "R76-1", edition 2006. Or id "R76", edition 2006, plus... there's no "part" field. I'll use id "R76-1" to be faithful. Hmm, but example says canonical "R60" not "OIML R 60". "R76-1" is the actual designation. I'll go "R76-1". Actually many treat R76 as the recommendation with parts 1 and 2. The certificate says "OIML R 76-1:2006". I'll use id "R76-1", edition 2006.

- accuracy_classes: ["II"]

Test reports:

Role "type_evaluation_report" seems apt for OIML test reports under scheme A. Both are test reports; NMi-3674610-01 (45 pages) and NMi-3674610-02 (19 pages). I'll set role "test_report" for both, or "type_evaluation_report". The certificate references "the OIML Test Report". I'll use "test_report".
